nameStory: Woolly foxglove gets its fuzzy name from the soft, woolly hairs that coat its leaves, giving them a distinctly fuzzy texture that you can feel when you gently touch them. The 'foxglove' part comes from the old belief that foxes would slip the tubular flowers over their paws like gloves to muffle their steps while hunting - though this charming tale is just folklore!
description: Woolly foxglove is a tall, striking wildflower that produces dense spikes of small, cream-colored to pale yellow tubular flowers. This European native stands 2-4 feet tall with a distinctive fuzzy appearance thanks to the woolly hairs covering its leaves. Unlike its more common purple cousin, this foxglove has a more subtle beauty with delicate, closely-packed blooms that create an impressive vertical display in summer.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves feel distinctly soft and woolly to the touch, covered in fine white hairs that give them a grayish-green, fuzzy appearance - this is the plant's signature feature

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small tubular flowers are cream to pale yellow, densely packed on tall spikes, much smaller and more numerous than purple foxglove's large drooping bells

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a basal rosette of fuzzy leaves in the first year, then sends up 2-4 foot tall flower spikes in the second year

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Flowering stems are sturdy and upright, also covered in the same woolly hairs as the leaves, feeling soft when touched

habitat: Woolly foxglove is quite rare in New England, occasionally found in disturbed areas, roadsides, and waste places where it has escaped cultivation. It prefers well-drained soils in sunny to partially shaded locations. This European native is not well-established in our region and is considered an uncommon escape from gardens.

seasonality.spring: Basal rosettes of woolly leaves emerge and can be identified by their distinctive fuzzy texture.
seasonality.summer: Tall flower spikes bloom with dense clusters of small cream or pale yellow tubular flowers, typically from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop while leaves begin to decline.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back as a biennial, leaving only dried stems and seed heads visible.

funFact: Despite being called 'woolly' for its fuzzy leaves, this plant is actually the source of the heart medication digoxin - the same woolly hairs that make it feel soft contain some of the highest concentrations of cardiac glycosides of any foxglove species!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with purple foxglove, but woolly foxglove's leaves are distinctly fuzzy and gray-green (not smooth and bright green), and its flowers are small, cream-colored, and densely packed (not large, purple, and drooping). Memory trick: 'Woolly = fuzzy leaves and tiny flowers.'
contextualKnowledge: All parts of woolly foxglove are extremely toxic and can cause serious heart problems, nausea, and vision issues if ingested. Never handle extensively without gloves, and keep away from children and pets. This plant is the source of the important heart medication digoxin, but should never be used for self-medication.
compareHints: Woolly foxglove stands out from other foxgloves by its distinctly fuzzy, grayish leaves and small, densely-packed cream flowers. Purple foxglove has large, drooping purple bells and smooth green leaves, while yellow foxglove has larger yellow flowers and lacks the woolly leaf texture. The woolly indumentum (fuzzy coating) is unique to this species among foxgloves you'll encounter in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Purple foxglove is the most common foxglove species in New England and the most likely to naturalize from gardens.
Yellow foxglove stands out from its more common cousin, purple foxglove, by its soft yellow color and larger individual blooms.

Among foxgloves in New England, straw foxglove is distinguished by its pale, cream-yellow flowers that are much smaller and more numerous than the large, bright yellow blooms of yellow foxglove (Digitalis grandiflora).
Among the foxglove family, Rusty Foxglove is unique for its rust-brown flowers - Purple Foxglove has pink-purple blooms, while Yellow Foxglove (rarely seen here) has pale yellow flowers.
